title: Design a Distributed API Rate Limiter
prompt: Design a distributed rate limiter that caps how many requests a client can make to an API — for example 1000 requests per minute per API key — enforced consistently across a fleet of API servers behind a load balancer.
blurb: Token bucket vs sliding window, Redis-backed counters, cross-node consistency, and fail-open vs fail-closed.

rubric.label: Requirements gathering
rubric.description: Separates functional (per-key limits, multiple tiers, response headers) from non-functional (low added latency, accuracy, availability, fail-mode).

rubric.label: Clarifying questions
rubric.description: Asks about limit granularity (key/IP/user/endpoint), accuracy tolerance, distributed vs per-node, latency budget, fail-open vs closed.

rubric.label: Algorithm choice
rubric.description: Token bucket, leaky bucket, fixed window, sliding window log, sliding window counter — tradeoffs of burst handling, memory, accuracy.

rubric.label: Estimations
rubric.description: Estimates QPS, number of keys, memory per counter, Redis ops/sec, added latency budget.

rubric.label: API & placement
rubric.description: Where the limiter sits (gateway/middleware/sidecar), the check contract, 429 responses and Retry-After/rate-limit headers.

rubric.label: State model
rubric.description: Counter/bucket keys, TTLs, per-window structure in Redis; atomic update via Lua/INCR.

rubric.label: High-level design
rubric.description: Request → limiter middleware → shared counter store → allow/deny; how counters are shared across nodes.

rubric.label: Cross-node consistency
rubric.description: Shared Redis vs local counters, atomic increments, race conditions, and the accuracy/latency tradeoff of centralization.

rubric.label: Fail-open vs fail-closed
rubric.description: What happens when the counter store is unreachable; graceful degradation, local fallback limits.

rubric.label: Scaling & hot keys
rubric.description: Sharding counters, hot-key (one abusive key) contention, local token pre-fetch, replication.

rubric.label: Observability
rubric.description: Throttle rate, near-limit clients, limiter latency, store errors.

functional_requirements: Enforce a request cap per client key over a time window (e.g. 1000/min)
Support multiple rules (per API key, per IP, per endpoint, per tier)
nonfunctional_requirements: Consistent enforcement across all API nodes
Highly available — a limiter outage must not take down the API
Reasonable accuracy (small over-admit tolerable, no large leaks)
clarifying_questions: What's the limit granularity — per API key, per user, per IP, per endpoint?
How strict — is a small over-count acceptable, or must it be exact?
Is this a global distributed limit or per-node?
What's the latency budget the limiter can add?
On limiter-store failure, do we fail open (allow) or fail closed (deny)?
qualifying_questions: Do we need burst allowance (token bucket) or smooth pacing (leaky bucket)?
How many distinct keys — thousands or hundreds of millions?

estimations.traffic: 1M req/s across the fleet; each request = 1 limiter check ≈ 1M Redis ops/s (mitigate with local batching)
estimations.keys: 10M active API keys; each bucket ~64B in Redis ≈ ~640MB, fits in memory easily
estimations.latency: Limiter must stay within a ~1-5ms budget; a same-AZ Redis round trip is sub-ms
estimations.sharding: 1M ops/s exceeds a single Redis node's comfort — shard by key or use a cluster

core_components: Limiter middleware/library in each API node (or API gateway)
Optional local token cache per node
data_model: Token bucket: key → {tokens, last_refill_ts}; refill computed lazily on access
Sliding-window counter: key → two fixed-window counts (current, previous) with weighting
Fixed window: key = bucket:{client}:{window_start}, INCR with EXPIRE = window
All keys carry TTL so expired windows self-clean
api_design: Internal check: allow(client_key, rule) → { allowed: bool, remaining, reset_ts }
On deny: HTTP 429 with Retry-After and X-RateLimit-Limit / X-RateLimit-Remaining / X-RateLimit-Reset headers
Admin: PUT /limits/{key} { rule } to set/override limits at runtime
reference.high_level_design: The limiter runs as middleware in each API node (or at the API gateway). On each request it derives the client key and rule, then executes an atomic update against a shared Redis store — ideally a Lua script that reads the bucket, refills tokens by elapsed time, decrements, and returns allow/deny in one round trip (avoiding read-modify-write races). If allowed, the request proceeds; if not, it returns 429 with headers. Counters carry TTLs to self-expire. To cut Redis load and latency, each node can pre-fetch a batch of tokens locally (approximate) and reconcile periodically. On Redis failure the limiter falls open (or to a conservative local limit) so the API stays up.

deep_dives.probe: Compare fixed-window vs sliding-window vs token bucket. Fixed window allows a 2x burst at the boundary — show me why, and how sliding-window-counter fixes it cheaply.
Ten API nodes hit the same key concurrently. How do you avoid a read-modify-write race so two nodes don't both admit the last token? Walk me through the atomic operation.
Redis is unreachable for 30 seconds. What does the limiter do — fail open, fail closed, or fall back to a local per-node limit? Justify the choice for an API.
One abusive key sends 500K req/s, all hashing to one Redis shard. That shard is now hot. How do you handle a single hot counter — local pre-decrement, sharded sub-counters, or shed early?
You cache limit-rule config locally with a TTL. When a popular rule's cache entry expires under load, how do you avoid every node stampeding the config store at once?
Limit rules live in a config database. How do you propagate a rule change to every node quickly — CDC/Debezium to a stream, pub/sub invalidation, or polling — and how fresh must it be?

followup_bank.question: Fixed window lets a client send 2x the limit across a window boundary. How do you fix that without the memory of a full sliding-window log?
How do you make token-bucket refill atomic across nodes so two servers don't both spend the last token?
How do you make the read-refill-decrement atomic — Lua script, INCR+EXPIRE, or WATCH/MULTI — and what are the race risks of each?
For cached limit rules, what's the eviction policy and how do you avoid a stampede on the config store when a hot rule expires?
How do rule changes propagate to nodes — CDC/Debezium to a stream vs pub/sub invalidation vs polling — and what staleness is acceptable?
Fail-open vs fail-closed when the counter store is down — which do you pick for a public API and why?
One key saturates a single shard. How do you spread or absorb that hot counter without losing accuracy?

scaling: Shard counters across a Redis Cluster by client key
Local token pre-fetch/batching per node to cut per-request round trips
Sub-counters (split a hot key into N shards, sum on read) for hot keys
Read replicas for config; counters are write-heavy so keep them on the primary/cluster
Approximate local limiting as a first cheap gate before the shared check
bottlenecks: Shared Redis becoming a per-request round-trip bottleneck
Hot key concentrating load on one shard
Config propagation lag on rule changes
Clock skew across nodes affecting window boundaries
tradeoffs: Centralized Redis (accurate, adds latency + SPOF risk) vs local per-node counters (fast, approximate, over-admits by node count)
Token bucket (allows bursts) vs leaky bucket (smooth pacing)
Sliding-window log (exact, memory-heavy) vs sliding-window counter (approximate, cheap)
Fail-open (availability, risk of abuse) vs fail-closed (safety, risk of outage)
Strict accuracy vs latency (local batching trades exactness for speed)
alternative_solutions: Envoy/API-gateway native rate limiting with a global rate-limit service (RLS)
Sidecar limiter (service mesh) instead of in-process middleware
Purely local token buckets with gossip reconciliation for approximate global limits
Cloud provider / CDN edge rate limiting for coarse protection
observability: Throttle rate (429s) per key/rule and overall
Counter-store error rate and fail-mode activations
security: Prevent key spoofing — derive client identity from authenticated credentials, not spoofable headers
Separate stricter limits for unauthenticated/IP-based traffic
Protect the admin config API with authz
Guard against limiter bypass if the store is down (bounded fail-open)
reference.reference_answer: A strong answer picks an algorithm deliberately — usually token bucket for burst tolerance or sliding-window-counter for boundary-accurate cheap limiting — and explains why fixed windows allow a 2x boundary burst. It centralizes state in Redis and makes the refill-decrement atomic via a Lua script to avoid read-modify-write races across nodes, while cutting round trips with local token pre-fetch/batching. It reasons explicitly about fail-open vs fail-closed for an API (usually bounded fail-open), handles hot keys with sub-counters or local pre-decrement, and gives 429s with Retry-After/X-RateLimit headers. It proactively raises the shared-store round trip, hot key, and config-propagation lag as bottlenecks, and covers rule distribution (CDC/pub-sub) and clock-skew on windows.

interviewer_notes: This is a mid-level question, so depth on the algorithm and the concurrency race is the key signal. Make them compare at least token bucket vs sliding window and articulate the fixed-window boundary-burst flaw. The decisive interrupt is the concurrency race — push until they describe an atomic Redis operation (Lua/INCR), not a naive GET-then-SET. Force a fail-open vs fail-closed decision with justification. If they mention a config database, fire the CDC/Debezium propagation probe; if they cache rules, fire the eviction/stampede probe. Hot key handling separates strong mid from senior.
